blocks.text: The True Identity of Thought is Analogy: The Mechanism of Creativity Revealed by Douglas Hofstadter
It is said that Isaac Newton discovered the universal law of gravitation when he saw an apple fall from a tree.
When we hear this episode, we imagine that some magical leap occurred inside the mind of a genius.
An ordinary person sees an apple and only thinks it looks delicious, but a genius flashes with the idea of gravity.
It seems like there is an insurmountable wall there.
However, Douglas Hofstadter, a cognitive scientist known for Gödel, Escher, Bach, asserts the following in his book Surfaces and Essences.
"There is no magic there. There is only analogy."
Today, I will introduce Hofstadter's theory, which explains the true identity of our thought and creativity in the most simple and powerful way.
1. Thinking is Searching for Similarities
Hofstadter's claim is radical.
He declares that the entire act of human thinking is analogy.
What is analogy?
It is superimposing an unknown matter in front of you onto a known matter in your past memories.
What happened inside Newton's head was not magic.
He found a common structure between the phenomenon of an apple falling to the ground happening in front of him and the phenomenon of the moon orbiting the earth in the sky.
Superficially, an apple and the moon are completely different. Their sizes, colors, and locations are different.
However, regarding the essential structure, that is, the point that they are being pulled toward the center by some force, aren't these two the same?
The moment he thought so, the great discovery that the laws of the ground can be applied to the universe was born.
According to Hofstadter, the processing taking place in the brain is the same for Einstein's theory of relativity and for deciding what to have for dinner today.
"This is similar to that thing I ate a long time ago."
This pattern recognition is exactly the true identity of intelligence.
2. Surfaces and Essences
Then, why can't we think like Newton?
It is because we are trapped by the Surface of things and cannot see the Essence.
For example, suppose you are a game developer.
When you think about wanting to make an interesting game like Mario, a person trapped by the surface thinks like this.
"Mario is a game where a plumber wearing a red hat jumps. So, let's make a game where an electrician wearing a blue hat jumps."
This is a superficial analogy. This will only result in a poor imitation.
On the other hand, a person who sees the essence extracts the structure of Mario.
"What is the essence of Mario? It is a sophisticated system where movement, attacking, and dodging are all solved by just one action of jumping."
If you can understand that, there is no need for the character to be a plumber, or even for the action to be jumping.

If you make a shooting game where you can attack, defend, and move with just one button operation, it might become a masterpiece that inherits the essence of Mario, even if it looks completely different.
This is the teaching of Surfaces and Essences preached by Hofstadter.
3. Creativity is Leaping Far
Creativity is not creating something from nothing.
It is the power to find a common essence from distant memories that seem completely unrelated at first glance.
If you make an analogy from a nearby memory, it becomes a common-sense idea.
If you make an analogy from a distant memory, it becomes an original idea.
Seeing the mechanism of an ant colony and seeing through to the common points with an urban traffic system.
Seeing the mechanism of biological evolution and applying it to a robot learning program.
These are all advanced analogies that ignore surface differences and extract only the essential structure.
It is, so to speak, the difference in the performance of the search engine in the brain.
Whether searching for "apple" only brings up "pear," or whether it can even get a hit for "moon."
The breadth of that search range is where a creator shows their skill.
4. The Moment of Enlightenment and Short Circuits
Looking back at history, there is a strange commonality in moments of great discovery or religious enlightenment.
That is, they are often triggered by extremely trivial, casual events.
Buddha, the founder of Buddhism, is said to have attained enlightenment the moment he saw the Morning Star shining in the sky at dawn after long training.
The Zen monk Kyogen Chikan attained enlightenment the moment a small stone hit a bamboo and made a clicking sound while he was cleaning the garden.
Archimedes of ancient Greece discovered the principle of buoyancy the moment he saw bathwater overflowing and shouted Eureka while naked.
Why do trivial stimuli like starlight or the sound of a pebble lead to world-changing discoveries?
Using Hofstadter's theory, this can also be explained.
Inside their brains, the network regarding the structure of the problem had been stretched to the limit by long-term deep thinking.
Then, information of a completely unrelated surface enters from the outside.
Usually, that trivial stimulus would be ignored.
However, it contacted the thought circuit stretched around inside the brain and played the role of a short circuit that forcibly connected concepts far apart.
The twinkling of stars, the sound of a pebble, overflowing hot water.
The physical structure hidden within them overlapped in an instant with the structure of the difficult problem they were holding.
In other words, enlightenment or inspiration might be a phenomenon like an electrical short circuit, where memories in extremely distant places in the brain connect with a snap sound through analogy.
5. Conclusion: Geniuses are Masters of Metaphor
Hofstadter's theory gives us courage.
When we cannot come up with ideas, we do not need to lament that we have no talent.
It might just be that the distance of the samples we are comparing is too close.
Read books from completely different fields, not just your own specialty, watch movies, and go on trips.
And always ask yourself this question.
"Is this phenomenon not the same structure as 'something' I know?"
Seeing the world through metaphor.
That is the only and strongest training for an ordinary person to approach the thinking of a genius.
